source.title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
source.authors: Xuyang Ge; Wentao Shu; Jia-Xing Wu; Yunhua Zhou; Zheng-Fu He; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse-dictionary analysis of superposition-related features to language-model pre-training snapshots, a new setting relative to toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper measures cross-snapshot feature directions, effective feature dimensionality, persistence, and temporal splitting. Introductory claims attributed to prior work are not treated as results. It does not test toy networks, neuron polysemanticity as a capacity mechanism, or whether natural features are intrinsically one- versus multi-dimensional.
record.test_reason: Applies Elhage et al.'s feature-dimensionality measure to crosscoder features in Pythia pre-training snapshots to measure superposition directly (Sec. 6, Fig. 8c). It also reports how feature splitting depends on dictionary size (App. F). Most other results use crosscoders as a tool to study training dynamics.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim attribution and ablation link feature evolution causally to downstream task performance: within tens of features they can disrupt or recover SVA, induction and IOI performance. IOI performance could not be fully recovered. They frame the dimensionality result as initialization features in weak superposition being compressed as emergent features arrive.
record.recipe_differences: The paper adapts sparse crosscoders to align features across language-model pre-training snapshots and measures feature evolution and dimensionality, rather than reproducing the original toy-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported proportion of activation-space dimensions depends on crosscoder dictionary size; the paper also reports that temporal splitting increases with dictionary size. Snapshot selection changes temporal resolution, while the authors report nearly identical overall trends with 16 versus 32 snapshots.

fits_no_version.finding: Most emergent features rotate sharply around step 1,000, leaving pre- and post-1,000 directions nearly orthogonal. Afterwards they rotate gradually.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature directions in LMs reorganize at a universal early turning point during pre-training.

fits_no_version.finding: Most emergent features persist for over 60% of snapshots after they form.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features learned during LM pre-training persist once formed.

fits_no_version.finding: Early training fits unigram/bigram statistics before sparse features emerge. Later-emerging features score higher on complexity (Pearson r = 0.309, p = 0.002).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LM pre-training has a statistical-learning phase followed by a feature-learning (superposition) phase.

record.problems: The analysis is limited to Pythia models and selected layers; the authors note that feature dimensionality in Pythia-6.9B may be limited by the crosscoder dictionary size. Feature splitting is described as rare in one analysis and is not quantified in the text. Broader generalization is left open.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result directly testing the listed claim versions was identified for extraction.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity-dependent phase transition or geometry tested.
No test of capacity competition or importance-based allocation of dimensions.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons examined.

Completeness (explained variance ~0.88-0.9 is reported, but not framed as a completeness test) and stability across seeds or methods for a fixed model are not tested. Only dictionary-size dependence of splitting is tested.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Crosscoder reconstruction: explained variance ~0.88-0.90 at L0 ~50-120 across dictionary sizes, comparable to per-snapshot SAEs. This bears on recoverability of sparse features and on completeness (~10% unexplained).
Decoder norm tracks linear probe separability: mean Pearson r = -0.867 (SD 0.153).
Two-phase feature pattern replicates across Pythia-160M seeds, Stanford CRFM GPT-2, the FineWeb-Edu dataset and 16 versus 32 snapshots. No dimensionality ratio is reported for these.

record.verdict_notes: Mainly a training-dynamics study using crosscoders as a tool. Its bearing on superposition versions is limited to the Sec. 6 dimensionality measure (V4) and the App. F dictionary-size splitting result (V5). R3 and R4 were relinked to none: cross-checkpoint stability is a property of the model, not evidence on whether dictionary units are canonical. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or sparsity-dependent transition in small networks are tested.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for capacity or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Does not establish that its extracted features cover all model features or generalize beyond the tested models and settings.
Does not establish that dictionary features are complete, method-independent canonical units; it studies cross-snapshot alignment and splitting.

Although it computes effective dimensionality using decoder directions, it does not compare naturally one-dimensional features with multi-dimensional features; each crosscoder latent is parameterized with decoder vectors.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Measured total crosscoder feature dimensionality relative to activation-space dimension over training.
rows.measure: Total feature dimensionality as a proportion of activation-space dimension
rows.value: First decreases, then increases around the turning point, eventually reaching approximately 70% of available dimensions.
rows.note: The paper interprets the trend as initialization features becoming compressed as emergent features form, followed by a feature-learning phase.
rows.check: Link stands. The baseline is not a control: the activation dimension is only the denominator of the ratio. The ~70% figure applies to the 98,304-feature (128x) crosscoder at the final snapshots.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3 experimental setup; Section 6, Equation 6 and Figure 8c.

rows.subject: Pythia-6.9B
rows.operation_detail: Measured total crosscoder feature dimensionality relative to activation-space dimension over training.
rows.measure: Total feature dimensionality as a proportion of activation-space dimension
rows.value: Shows the same decrease-then-increase trend as Pythia-160M, but accounts for a smaller proportion of activation-space dimensions; the authors suggest the limited crosscoder feature count may explain this.
rows.note: The text gives no exact proportion for this model.
rows.check: No numeric proportion is given in the text; it can only be read from Fig. 8c. The authors attribute the lower ratio to the 32,768-feature dictionary size, a method choice, not to the model.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V4. Sparse crosscoder features are recovered in Pythia-6.9B. Their dimensionality ratio follows the same decrease-then-increase trend as Pythia-160M, with a smaller proportion of activation dimensions. Limited crosscoder capacity is the authors' proposed explanation; no exact proportion is stated.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3 experimental setup; Section 6, paragraph following Equation 6 and Figure 8c.
source_check.problem: Lower dimensional coverage does not make V4 partial: V4 specifies neither complete coverage nor a minimum recovered proportion.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature decoder directions across training snapshots using projections.
rows.measure: Projection/cosine similarity of feature directions across snapshots
rows.value: Most features undergo drastic directional shifts around step 1,000, leaving pre- and post-step 1,000 directions nearly orthogonal; later rotation is more gradual, and final directions retain notable cosine similarity to their initial post-step 1,000 orientations.
rows.note: Aggregate description of most features; exact projection values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Directional rotation of features across training checkpoints is a property of the model's learning dynamics. It is not evidence on whether dictionary features are complete, stable or canonical units of a given model. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Measured persistence of emergent crosscoder features using a decoder-norm threshold.
rows.measure: Feature lifetime as a proportion of snapshots
rows.value: Most emergent features persist for above 60% of snapshots after formation.
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence that learned features persist and that crosscoders track them across snapshots.
rows.check: Persistence of features across training snapshots describes training dynamics, and partly validates the crosscoder. It does not test V5's canonicity or stability across dictionaries. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Searched for similar feature decoder vectors across crosscoders with different dictionary sizes to assess temporal feature splitting.

conditions.value: long sequences containing repeated text patterns

rows.measure: Number of distinct crosscoder features representing a similar concept across training
rows.value: The number of distinct features increases with dictionary size; at each snapshot after step 2,000, almost exactly one feature represents the concept.
rows.note: The authors identify this as temporal feature splitting: a concept is represented by different features at different training stages.
rows.check: Measured on one example concept (repeated-text/induction feature, Fig. 24). Each snapshot after step 2,000 has about one matching feature, but the number of distinct latents grows from 3 (6,144 features) to 8 (98,304 features). The unit therefore depends on dictionary size.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Examined which crosscoder features exhibit temporal splitting and their activation patterns.
rows.measure: Association between temporal feature splitting and activation density
rows.value: Temporal feature splitting predominantly occurs among densely activating features; the authors suggest subtly different activation patterns across training may account for it.
rows.note: The text describes this as a qualitative pattern, without a stated count or effect size.
rows.check: Qualitative statement with no counts. The authors call temporal splitting rare overall (Sec. 3), concentrated among densely activating features.

relationships.reason: Total feature dimensionality falls, then rises to ~70% of activation dimensions, consistent with sparse features stored in superposition (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Total feature dimensionality first fell, then rose to about 70% of activation dimensions, consistent with sparse features stored in superposition.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R1 agrees with Section 6: recovered sparse features have total dimensionality that decreases and then increases, eventually reaching approximately 70% of activation dimensions.

relationships.reason: Same trend, but features cover a smaller share of dimensions; authors attribute this to limited dictionary size, so the measure depends on the method (R2).
relationships.display_finding: The crosscoder showed the same trend, but its features covered a smaller share of dimensions, which the authors attribute to limited dictionary size.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R2 reports recovered features and the same dimensionality trend. Lower coverage, tentatively attributed to dictionary capacity, does not qualify V4, which makes no completeness or coverage guarantee.

relationships.condition: Pythia-160M layer 6, dictionary sizes 6,144-98,304, densely activating features
relationships.reason: One concept splits into more distinct latents as dictionary size grows (3 to 8 in Fig. 24), mainly among dense features; the units are not canonical (R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: One concept split from 3 into 8 distinct latents as dictionary size grew, mainly among dense features.

source_check.reason: Appendix F and Figure 24 support the result attributed to R5/R6: the illustrated concept splits into more temporal latents as dictionary size increases, with three labeled latents at 6,144 features and eight at 98,304. Splitting predominantly affects densely activating features, qualifying dictionary-unit stability and canonicity.

relation.reason: Section 6 reports feature-dimensionality measurements bearing on V4, and Appendix F reports dictionary-size-dependent temporal splitting bearing on V5.

tranche.reason: The study measures superposition-related feature dimensionality in the new setting of language-model pre-training trajectories, using crosscoder features rather than ground-truth toy-model features.

source_check.notes: The dimensionality metric uses learned crosscoder features, not ground-truth features; activation-space dimension is its denominator, not a control. Appendix F concerns splitting across training stages, with almost one representative feature active per snapshot after step 2,000.

statements.correction: Pythia-6.9B layer 16; 32,768-feature crosscoder; lower dimensionality ratio than Pythia-160M; same decrease-then-increase trend; limited dictionary capacity proposed as likely explanation; no exact ratio stated.
statements.problem: The lower coverage is reported, but dictionary capacity is a tentative explanation. This measurement limitation does not establish a limitation of V4's claim that recoverable sparse features exist.
